newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Lower car quotas to impact Singapore's C&C.
newsitem.headline: Lower car quotas to impact Singapore's C&C.

text.p: Lower car quotas last year are likely to pull the 1996 profit growth of Singapore's leading car distributor Cycle & Carriage Ltd (C&C) down to single digits, analysts said on Monday.
The group, agent for Mercedes-Benz cars and other brands, is expected to release its 1996 earnings on Wednesday.
C&C's share price has shed 18 percent from a high of S$17.90 near the start of the year. It was hovering around S$14.60 on Monday, down 20 cents on the day.
"The market expectation for C&C has come down a lot recently and the share price is getting hammered," said David Leow, investment analyst with HSBC James Capel.
The latest analyst consensus forecast in The Estimate Directory is S$194.9 million in net profit for 1996, down more than five percent from about six months ago.
While the 1996 estimate still shows seven percent growth in earnings over the previous year, the growth pales in comparison with the 47 percent rise of 1995.
Analysts said one of the main factors for the lower growth was that the government had released fewer certificates of entitlements in 1996.
In Singapore, new car buyers have to secure a COE through a bidding system before they can buy a car.
Danielle Yew, investment analyst with Goldman Sachs, said the COEs released for cars in 1996 were 16 percent lower than the previous year's 27,376.
She said the lower quota would also have an impact on the earnings of Inchcape, which distributes Toyotas, and Intraco, the agent for Rover cars.

Motor distributors, especially C&C, have also been hit hard by parallel importers -- importing outside the authorised dealing system -- and by aggressive marketing by Sime Singapore, the agent for BMWs.
Leow said: "Sime has been cutting prices for BMW cars by S$10,000 a car to get market share. Parallel importers are also taking business away from C&C."
Parallel imports of Mercedes more than doubled to about 14 percent in 1996 from 5.5 percent the previous year. Analysts said they expected parallel imports to continue growing.
"The market is also waiting to see how parallel imports have affected C&C margins," said Yew.
Besides motor distribution, which accounts for about 70 percent of C&C's earnings, the contribution from property development, which accounts for the rest, is expected to be steady.
Looking forward, Leow said group earnings this year would continue to be affected by expected low car quotas and by the subdued property market.
